authoredPrompt: This figure pairs a three-step reaction scheme with electrostatic potential maps to follow an SN2 substitution, arranged in three stacked rows with the maps on the left and the structures on the right. The top row writes Nu:- in magenta, a plus sign, and a tetrahedral carbon drawn with one bold wedge, one hashed bond, and two plain bonds, joined to a magenta X; alongside it the maps show the free nucleophile as an isolated deep red sphere and the alkyl halide as a two-lobed surface labeled "Tetrahedral" whose halide end is also red. A downward arrow leads to the middle row, where the transition state sits inside square brackets with Nu at the left and X at the right, each carrying a magenta delta- and each tied to the central carbon by a dotted line while the remaining three bonds to that carbon lie in a plane; its map is a wide, symmetric three-lobed surface labeled "Planar", red at both ends and green and yellow across the middle. A second arrow reaches the product row, Nu-C with the wedge and hash now reversed, plus X:-, mapped as a lobed Nu-bearing surface labeled "Tetrahedral" beside a separate red halide sphere. Read down the column, the color scale tracks negative charge leaving the nucleophile, spreading over both ends of the planar species, and settling on the departing halide. The layout supports a single-step mechanism in which backside attack 180 degrees from the leaving group turns the carbon's substituents inside out.
authoredInteractions: - Slider for reaction progress: drag from reactants through the bracketed transition state to products, and the geometry morphs from tetrahedral to planar and back while the red electrostatic potential shifts from nucleophile to both ends to leaving group, making charge delocalization during one-step SN2 substitution clear.
authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, the SN2 reaction occurs when an electron pair on the nucleophile Nu:– forces out the group X:–, which takes with it the electron pair from the former C–X bond. This occurs through a transition state in which the new Nu–C bond is partially formed at the same time that the old C–X bond is partially broken and in which the negative charge is shared by both the incoming nucleophile and the outgoing halide ion. The transition state for this inversion has the remaining three bonds to carbon in a planar arrangement (the figure).

The transition state of an SN2 reaction has a planar arrangement of the carbon atom and the remaining three groups. Electrostatic potential maps show that negative charge is delocalized in the transition state.

The figure shows the S N 2 reaction along with their ball-and-stick model in electrostatic potential maps. Tertiary alkyl halide and substituted compound are tetrahedral, while transition state is planar.

The mechanism proposed by Hughes and Ingold is fully consistent with experimental results, explaining both stereochemical and kinetic data. Thus, the requirement for a backside approach of the entering nucleophile (180° away from the departing X group) causes the stereochemistry of the substrate to invert, much like an umbrella turning inside-out in the wind. The Hughes–Ingold mechanism also explains why second-order kinetics are observed: the SN2 reaction occurs in a single step that involves both alkyl halide and nucleophile. Two molecules are involved in the step whose rate is measured.

discrepancies: The electrostatic potential maps in the generated figure are completely opaque and lack the inner ball-and-stick molecular structure visible in the source.
The chemical structure in the generated figure is missing the terminal atoms (ligands/hydrogens) on the three non-reacting bonds.
The source uses stereochemical wedge and dash notation to show out-of-plane bonds, whereas the generated figure uses generic solid cylinders.
The forming and breaking bonds in the transition state are shown as dashed lines in the source, but as solid transparent cylinders in the generated figure.
The original figure lays out the three reaction stages vertically simultaneously, whereas the generated figure collapses them into a single animated view controlled by a slider.
evaluation.notes: The interactive slider is a fantastic pedagogical adaptation of the static figure, but the rendering is heavily simplified, lacking the translucent EPM surfaces, stereochemical wedge/dash bonds, and terminal atoms.
action_items: Make the EPM shader material translucent and add internal ball-and-stick models for the atoms and bonds inside it to match the source.
Add small spheres at the ends of the C-H bonds in the chemical structure to represent the hydrogen atoms/ligands.
Replace the solid transparent cylinders for the forming/breaking bonds with a dashed line geometry or shader to properly denote partial bonds.
Implement wedge and dash visual styling for the out-of-plane bonds in the chemical structure to accurately depict stereochemistry.
